items.title: Player interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2012
items.q: That’s when my friend Hank Leo called me up and asked me what was going on with me and if I’d be interested in coming up and working with the Y, with the music program with the kids here.

ctx.x: Yeah. I mean I think so. You know, after the storm, and even when the city was officially back up and running, there wasn’t much work for musicians at the time, you know, because there weren’t very many tourists coming to the city. And most people know that

in New Orleans it’s I think mostly the economy is based on tourism. And so yeah, I had to try to find an alternate, some other things to do. I was doing some touring, on the road and everything, and that was mostly when there was a lot of publicity about the hurricane. I mean people obviously were doing what they could to help people from New Orleans in other parts of the country. So there were a lot of musical engagements and performances to help raise money and funds for victims of Hurricane Katrina. And so I…

Yesterday you played in Utica. And I was wondering, because both you and your drummer were talking about how joyful and active this New Orleans music is. And is it different to perform for an audience that maybe isn’t as engaged as an audience in New Orleans might be?
